rpc: report the worker host's CPU, disk and RAM on the stats reply

The Monitor's CPU and Disk read cards show only the coordinator, because the worker's
RPC stats reply carries GPU telemetry and nothing about the machine that GPU sits in.
A worker that is swapping its weights off disk looks idle from the coordinator.

Add a worker-side sampler over procfs and append its readings to the gpu_monitor object
that the reply already returns, so the worker's CPU percent, disk read and write, RAM and
CPU model ride the same line as its GPU temperature and PCIe link. The string is passed
through Op::stats and RPCMETRICS unchanged, so no client, coordinator or server route
changes. A daemon thread reads procfs once a second, only when the RPC monitor flag is
set: a run without the flag starts no thread and reads nothing. The first reply answers
with the identity and RAM, since a rate needs two readings.

Readings follow the coordinator's sampler (serve/telemetry.py) so the two hosts compare:
/proc/stat busy share, MemTotal minus MemAvailable, and whole-device disk bytes summed the
way psutil.disk_io_counters() does - a device counts when /sys/block lists it, so
partitions are skipped and loop devices count. A /proc/diskstats line with fewer than
seven stat fields adds nothing, and a CPU model name is escaped so it cannot break the
JSON line.

engine: drain the peer GPU at sync points; bounded, backed-off doorbell waits

Two GPUs: the end of a prompt and every checkpoint waited only for device
0, so the peer's queued work (prompt ring copies of unpicked experts, its
decode and refill streams) could still be running. Prefill now drains the
peer's streams before it returns (bounded, like the layer-split helper's,
which used unbounded syncs), and checkpoints call PeerExperts::drain().

The GPU-side doorbell waits (wait_flag_ge, wait_flag_ge_or, doorbell_wait)
polled mapped host memory every 100 ns with no limit, for as long as the
host took - with a peer, the slower card's rows on every layer. The pause
now doubles up to STRATA_SPIN_MAX_NS (default 2000; 100 = the old poll),
and past STRATA_SPIN_TIMEOUT_S (default the host GPU wait limit + 10 s) a
wait gives up and counts itself in word 8 of its flag block; the host
checks it after each window or token and fails that output with an error.

ds41 RAM tier: prefetch() reads guessed experts ahead of admit()

The router lookahead guesses the next layer's experts while the CPU works on
this one. With the adaptive RAM tier, misses are read with O_DIRECT, so warmed
file pages do not help. prefetch() reads the guesses into free RAM slots on a

expert instead of reading it again. A guess that no admit() asked for enters
the tier at end_step(), as an admitted expert. A failed read frees its slot.
prefetch() starts nothing between end_step() and open_prefetch(), because the
slots change between steps.

ds41 prefetch: the DMA copier never skips a layer (a skipped layer computed garbage)

The copy thread took the lowest planned layer above the last copied one from
the two parity tags, read once each. Descheduled between the two reads (32 CPU
threads on the laptop), it read tag 0 before layer l's plan landed and tag 1
after layer l + 1's, took l + 1, and never copied l: its done flag let the
GPU compute layer l's guessed experts from a stale buffer. The hidden state
went bad, every router score became NaN, all six ids were 384, and the CPU
side failed with "moe_mul1: bad expert" and an illegal memory access (3 of 3

detail::next_copy_layer reads the other parity's tag again once it has a
candidate: plans run in layer order on one stream, each tag after a system
fence, so the second read sees the earlier layer. No later plan can overwrite
that tag first, since it waits for the earlier layer's copy.

The copy kernel reads host memory with SM loads and slows every main-stream

new epoch before each step, so a flag of an earlier step never matches. A
failed copy still raises the flag, and the step then throws.

ds41 host experts: the adaptive RAM tier (keep what a miss reads)

With enable_adapt(N), N slots of each capacity stay free. admit() reads an
expert that is in no tier into a free slot (O_DIRECT, 1 MiB parts on up
to 8 threads) and points the CPU kernel at it. end_step() publishes the
new experts, records the step's routes as uses, and frees the least
recently used slots until each capacity has N free again. During a step
only free slots are written, so no reader sees a slot change.

The VRAM tier locks the RAM slot of a swap in flight, and releases the
RAM slot of an expert that a miss read in while its swap ran. An expert
written back from VRAM gets a fresh age (Codex review of cache_sim).

Compress checkpoint state on disk and optionally thin checkpoints

A checkpoint is 36 GDN rows of fp32 (S: 128x48x128 = 3 MiB and conv history
10240x3, 120 KiB) plus PLE history and indexer tails: ~118 MB, of which the
recurrence S is 96%.  The engine holds it in fp32, so nothing is stored at a
higher precision than it is computed in, and none of it is derivable from what
else the file holds.

Measured on a real 70768-token file (7 states, 824 MB):
- zstd -1 raw 0.941, lz4 1.004: the low mantissa bytes are noise
- byte-shuffled (4 planes) zstd -1 0.856 at ~1 GB/s, decompress ~2.4 GB/s
- XOR with the previous checkpoint first: no gain (0.854); consecutive states
  differ by 40-80% (relative norm), only 0.01% of floats are equal
- K/V int8 compresses 4-8%: left raw

Format 2 now stores gdn and ple byte-shuffled and zstd -1 compressed when the
build has zstd (found by CMake, optional; without it files are raw and a
compressed one is refused, never misread).  A turn's delta on the real file
goes from 267.5 MB to 233.5 MB, a whole file from 1643 MB to 1558 MB.

--conversation-dir-checkpoint-gap N (default 0 = all) writes only the root,
the two deepest and the checkpoints whose loss would make a request resume
more than N tokens earlier.  The file name is taken from the thinned image, so
a reloaded conversation maps to the same file.

Write a parked conversation as a delta of a file it shares pages with

--conversation-dir rewrote a whole ~2 GB image for every new turn.  Format 2
lets a file name a parent in the same directory and hold only what differs:
per layer and K/V buffer the bytes past the longest run of matching 64 KiB
chunks, and the checkpoints (GDN/PLE/tails) the parent does not hold.  Every
format 2 file ends with an index (XXH64 per chunk and per checkpoint, the
chain's depth and sizes); a writer reads it to choose the parent without
loading images, and a reader checks the restored image against it, so a delta
whose parent changed, went missing or rotted is rejected, never applied.

Matching by chunk hash, not by token prefix, also catches the common case
where the client re-rendered the reply's tail (#342): the shared prefix is
reused even though the old tokens are not a prefix of the new ones.

A chain deeper than 8 or whose deltas pass half the base is written whole.
Persist writes files, fsyncs the directory, writes conversations.manifest
(the held files), then removes conv-* files neither held nor an ancestor of a
held one.  load_all skips files kept only as an ancestor and admits a delta by
its restored size.  Format 1 files still read; the shipped binary cannot read
format 2.

On two real files (61637 and 70768 tokens, siblings sharing 59173 tokens) the
child's delta is 889 MB of 1908 MB and restores byte for byte; against the
same conversation cut back one turn it is 268 MB.  The live state and every new
checkpoint are ~118 MB of GDN each and are written whole: they dominate.

native experts: IQ3_S takes the AVX-2 kernel for one token too where its grid is gathered

#152's rule gives a lone token's gate/up rows to ggml's dot, because the multi-token kernels were no faster at one
token. With the gathered decode that no longer holds for IQ3_S on the Intel cores that gather it: an expert's gate/up
rows for one token on an i9-14900KF P-core take 0.34 ms with ggml's dot and 0.19 ms with the AVX-2 kernel. And in
decode most CPU experts serve one token of the window.

So on a CPU without AVX-512 where cpu_gather_fast() holds (Intel, Alder Lake or later, see the gather commit) and
STRATA_IQ256_GATHER is not 0, IQ3_S takes the multi-token kernel from one token on. This only pays together with the
gathered decode: on the same CPU's E-cores, which keep the scalar decode, it is 0.71 -> 0.68 ms, about even. That is
why it follows the gather's machine-wide rule and not the per-thread one. Measured in the engine with Swift 1.5
IQ3_XXS (whose IQ3_S layers this reaches): the CPU expert time per verify window -4%.

This changes results. A lone token's IQ3_S gate/up rows now round like the multi-token kernel's (the order of the
float additions), no longer like ggml's dot. They are the same rows the token gets in a group, so on these CPUs IQ3_S
experts no longer depend on how many drafts a window held (#152), and every core rounds them alike. Down rows and
the other formats keep the default rule. STRATA_IQ_MT_MIN set (2 is the old default) keeps its rule for every format.

The decision is native_gu_mt_min(): every probe is in expert_layout.cpp and cpu_avx2_ok() comes first. Nothing
compiled for AVX2 runs before that check, including on an older-CPU build (STRATA_ISA_FLOOR) on an AVX-only CPU.
iq_avx2_parity checks native_gu_rows wherever native_gu_mt_min is 1: each token's rows must match alone and in groups

cpu kernels: AVX-VNNI forms of the AVX-2 i-quant, IQ4_NL and Q2_0 rows (cpu_avxvnni_ok)

Alder Lake, Sapphire Rapids and later have AVX-VNNI on every core: vpdpwssd does the madd and the add of an i-quant
row in one uop, and vpdpbusd the maddubs + madd(ones) of the IQ4_NL and Q2_0 down rows. The sums are integer, so the
results are bit for bit those of the AVX2 forms: vpdpwssd wraps like madd + add, and the maddubs it replaces in the
down rows cannot saturate (IQ4_NL |w| <= 127, Q2_0 codes 0..3).

The row kernels move to iq_avx2_rows.inl and q2_avx2_rows.inl, which iq_avx2.cpp and q2_avx2.cpp include twice: once
as they were (namespace plain) and once with AVX-VNNI (namespace vnni). In the second copy every function is declared
with target("avxvnni") under GCC/Clang, so the intrinsics compile there and nowhere else: neither file gets
-mavxvnni, which would let the compiler use the extension in the plain path. MSVC takes the intrinsics under
/arch:AVX2. CMake checks that the compiler has them (GCC 11, Clang 12) and otherwise builds without the copies
(STRATA_AVXVNNI=0).

cpu_avxvnni_ok() in expert_layout.cpp, which is not compiled for AVX2: cpu_avx2_ok() and CPUID 7.1:EAX[4], off under
STRATA_FORCE_ISA (a CPU that stops at AVX2), off in a STRATA_ISA_FLOOR build, and STRATA_NO_AVXVNNI=1 turns it off.
The VNNI copies are reached only through the AVX2 kernels' entry points, which the engine already calls only behind
cpu_avx2_ok().

dd24a55 reads the IQ3 grid words with one gather under STRATA_IQ256_GATHER=1, on every core, and keeps it off by

- IQ3_XXS: the four even-sign masks by one 64-bit gather as well;

layer split: score every four-way placement instead of guessing it

A four-GPU run picked its split from a formula that reads only `layer_ms`
(SMs x clock) and shares the layers in proportion to speed; the free VRAM
that decides how many experts a stage can actually hold never entered it,
so the search could hand the most layers to the card with the least room
and never notice.  All C(L-3,3) placements are now scored - 15,180 at 48
layers - and 2,068 of them cost nothing extra, because a stage's fill
depends only on its own layer range and its own free VRAM: `predict`
already hands each ranked pair to the one stage that owns its layer and
stops each stage at its first pair that does not fit, so a range is walked
once and memoised.

The cost model's mass curve changes with it.  `mass[r]` was (r+1)^-1.2,
fitted to the 5080+3090 sweep - still right on that rig (99.35% predicted
at 20,000 held, 99.4% measured) and wrong on IQ3_S, where it claims the
top 5,805 pairs hold 94.9% of the routed mass and the rig measures 69.2%
over four boots and 14.9M decode lookups.  No exponent reconciles them,
because the curve is a property of the model's routing and the profile
carries only a ranking, with no counts.  The mass is now the increment of
H(f) = 1 - (1 - f)^b over the held fraction, whose prefixes sum to exactly
H(N/total); b = 3 (STRATA_SPLIT_COVER_B overrides it) is chosen to leave
the validated regime where it was - at f = 0.8138 it gives the old fit's
99.35% - while at f = 0.59 it gives 93.2% against 92.2% measured.

This is the placement search from #584, carried on v0.1.39 and without the
weight carve it rode in on: v0.1.39 ships its own carve (#559 / #639), and
the search only runs under `--layer-split auto`, where nothing is carved -
so `cap[i]` is already net of the dense weights and a stage's room is what
`predict` already subtracts, its session.

Measured on the 4-way IQ3_S rig (2x RTX 3060 + 2x RTX 5060), same config and
same flags in both arms, the binary the only difference: the four-way split
moves from K=10,19,34 to K=14,31,41, the prompt chunk the starved cards allow
grows 768 -> 1280 tokens, prefill goes 425 -> 597 tok/s (+40%) and decode
44 -> 51 tok/s (+16%), with the decode expert-cache hit 74.7% -> 83.3%.  Two
boots per arm, and the split is deterministic.  The curve and the search are
one commit, so that measures the pair, not the search alone.

Elastic K/V (--kv-grow): the K/V takes VRAM as the context grows, the expert cache holds the rest

At --max-context 262144 the K/V is allocated whole at start (3.35 GiB at int8 with the drafter's) and the expert
cache is sized around it. With --kv-grow (or STRATA_KV_GROW=1) the K/V pools and the cache arena are CUDA VMM ranges
(core/vmm.hpp; the driver calls through the runtime's entry-point query, nothing links the driver library). The K/V
maps 2 MiB chunks for the cells the requests reach (16384 at start); when a request needs more, slots just below the
prompt path's loan give theirs up, a hotter expert in them first moving into the slot of the coldest one in the loan
region. A short request after a long one hands the chunks back and the slots refill from the profile. No address
moves, so no graph is captured again, and --max-context cells always fit.

- serve: grows at a request (its prompt, and a parked conversation before its restore) and in the decode rounds;
  trims once the outgoing session is parked
- generate: grows once for the prompt and max_new, before the loan
- one GPU with a profile, the whole K/V in VRAM (no --kv-resident), every expert in RAM (not the low-RAM tier);
  STRATA_KV_GROW_INIT / _STEP / _FLOOR for tests. Off by default: more slots move experts between GPU and CPU.

prefill: the dense GGUF projections through MMQ on HIP (opt-in STRATA_DENSE_MMQ=1), the K-quant instances on the HIP build

The prompt path's dense projections (attention qkv/gate, the PLE key, the shared
experts, the router, the head) run dequantize-to-FP16 + cuBLAS: on the RDNA2
cards that is 68% of the prefill GPU time at ~25% of the card's fp32-accumulate
rate, while the same shapes through llama.cpp's int8 MMQ run ~7x faster
(measured with bench_dense_gemm).  This wires Gemm::native's beta = 0 products
through the MMQ path the MoE experts already take: quantize the FP16 activations
to q8_1 (they are converted to FP32 in the dequant scratch, which the old path
only fills afterwards) and run one mul_mat_q product per 1024-row chunk.  It is
opt-in (STRATA_DENSE_MMQ=1; unset, nothing changes) and falls back silently to
the old path on any shape MMQ does not take.

- STRATA_MMQ_KQUANTS also compiles the Q4_K / Q5_K / Q5_1 / Q6_K instances on
  the HIP branch (the mixed-quant packs' dense tensors are K-quants: this
  model's attention/PLE matrices are IQ4_XS/IQ3_S/Q4_K/Q5_K/Q6_K), adds Q6_K to
  the CUDA list, and defines STRATA_MMQ_KQUANTS for the HIP target.
- Gemm::native_mmq: one MMQ context, xq/ident/bounds buffer (~9.5 MB) and a
  failed-flag per Gemm; fp16->fp32 and the {0, rows} bounds helper join
  moe_mmq's kernel set.
- K must be a full 256-value multiple.  MMQ loads the weights in 256-value K
  chunks, and past a partial row the chunk reads bytes past the row - the next
  row's, or for the last weight row bytes past the tensor, which no caller
  guarantees to be zeros (the MoE path is safe because its gather buffers end
  in a zeroed tail).  On this pack the 640-value IQ4_NL shared-expert down
  picked up a NaN scale from the next tensor's blocks and zeroed the output;
  the odd shapes stay on the dequantize + cuBLAS path.

codebook lookups, and the 26.8 GiB per_layer_token_embd table reads only

What it is: the threshold where nearly every tensor in the file belongs
to the GPU's buffer and llama.cpp maps the file into it instead of
copying the GPU's weights out (metal-split-mmap.patch does the copying
below it).  Q2_0, -c 32768: 44 layers 23.8 tok/s, 32.2 GiB footprint,

So a model that nearly fits a Mac wants every layer on the GPU and a
context that fits, not the layer tuner's split - the opposite of the
right answer for Kolibri-1, which does not fit at all.

Layer split: pipelined verify windows (--pipeline-windows, opt-in)

With a split the two cards take turns on every verify window: stage 0 runs its
layers and hands off, then waits while stage 1 runs the rest, the head and the
draft. The batch pipeline (--batch-groups) overlaps different conversations;
one conversation's decode stayed serial.

--pipeline-windows 2 runs window K+1 on stage 0 while stage 1 verifies window
K. The guess for K+1 comes from the MTP chain, launched as soon as K's verdict
is known and teacher-forced through K+1's drafts: if K is accepted as guessed,
K+1 is already half done; if not, stage 0 restores its GDN state from a
snapshot, replays K's commit with the real count, and K+1 is rebuilt from the
real tokens. --pipeline-windows 1 overlaps only the prompt's short reads
through the windows (--short-read). Default 0: nothing changes.

What it adds:
- Verifier: a non-blocking form of run()/commit() (capture_all, pl_launch,
  prestage, service, done, pl_finish, pl_commit_async), the batch pipeline's
  batch_launch/batch_poll pattern for one sequence. The window, its staging,
  the PLE gather at layer 0, the zero-doorbell graph's flag, the #267 release
  on a timeout and the commit graph are run()'s. Two verifiers per stage (one
  per window parity) share one stream of their card (set_stream) and each
  pair has its own hand-off.
- set_always_publish: the pipelined verifiers copy the token rows to the host
  at every layer, because the adaptive tier now marks experts evicted on the
  host while windows are in flight, before the device residency table follows.
- MtpDrafter: chain_launch (the round and its steps back to back, an event
  after each output, the first steps fed the in-flight window's drafts by a
  one-thread forcing kernel), prefill without a host sync, 8 rows with 2, the
  drafter's stream at the highest priority (CUDA only).
- the adaptive tier beside the pipeline: evictions are marked first, then the
  refill copies wait (on the tier's thread) for every window in flight; the
  RAM side of a swap (exchange, release, unpin) waits for the windows that may
  still pull the incoming experts over PCIe.
- an agreement gate: a speculative window is launched only when the chain's
  estimate says it is likely kept (STRATA_PIPELINE_THETA, default 0.2); a
  window known to be wrong gets empty plans for its remaining layers; a lookup
  window's continuation becomes the speculative window behind it.
- VRAM: 160 MiB more kept out of each card's cache for the second verifier,
  and the two GDN snapshots on the first card.
- off, with one log line saying why, for anything it does not support: --batch
  slots, --peer-device, the helper caches, three or more stages, a split on
  one GPU, no drafter. Requests with repetition penalties or coupled draft
  sampling decode serially. Nothing is in flight outside the two pipelined
  loops, so checkpoints, parking and the serial paths are unchanged.

Asynchronous adaptive expert tier (--adapt-async 1, opt-in)

In the resident RAM mode (--resident-experts) an adaptive round runs on a
thread the decode loop joins after the draft: choose, copy the evicted slots
back with a stream sync, copy the new experts in from the RAM copy (through
the driver's staging when it is pageable). With ~90 swaps that was ~24 ms
every 4th window (measured on our fork). --adapt-async 1 splits a round into
four steps that advance between windows on a helper thread, so no window
waits for one:

  1. choose (adapt()'s rule, over snapshots of the counts and the residency)
     and copy the evicted slots back (D2H), each from the cache of the card
     that owns its layer
  2. stage the exchanges, mark the evicted experts non-resident (the CPU reads
     them from the exchange buffers), copy the new experts in: straight from
     a page-locked RAM copy, else through a pinned bounce buffer
  3. mark the new experts resident, move the evicted blobs into the RAM places
     the new ones left
  4. flip the copy's offsets

A slot is overwritten only after its old expert stopped being planned for the
GPU, and a RAM place is reused only once its expert is resident. The residency
tables on the devices are uploaded at steps 2 and 3, as apply_pending does
(the verify graph's doorbell reads them). A request starts with the round
drained, before its prompt lends any slot. --expert-profile-save counts the
routing at the start of each round, as the blocking tier does. Swaps that
need no exchange (the evicted expert is in the RAM copy already, or the new
one is not: a RAM budget) take the same steps without a copy back; a new
expert outside the RAM copy is read from the files on the helper thread.

Default off: which window first computes a swapped-in expert on the GPU
depends on when its copy lands, so the tier is not bit-exact from run to run.
Without the flag nothing changes. With it, the blocking tier still runs
outside --serve, without the resident RAM copy, and with --batch slots,
--peer-device or --remote-expert-opt (said once at startup). The exchange
buffers are twice as many with it (the bounce half): 96 more blob-sized
pinned buffers, ~130 MiB with 1.38 MB blobs.

Layer split (with the resident mode on a split, #848): each swap's copies run
on the owning card's refill stream under that card's device; the homes are
looked up the way #848's resident_stage_swaps does.

Measured: Swift 1.5 IQ3_XXS at 160K (q4_0 KV), i9-14900KF, 32 GB of RAM,

bench(macos): a GPU layer count has to be measured in the server

Measuring llama-server on its own says Kolibri-1 Q4_K_M wants 30 GPU
layers on a 48 GB M5 Pro and runs at 43-48 tok/s.  Measured through
serve/server.py, the same prompts and the same count give 16-22, and
the best count is the 1-5 the standalone tool rates slowest:

  GPU layers   llama-server alone   in the server
           1                 32.0   32.2
           5          not measured  32.4
           9           28.3, 26.1   26.5 - 28.3
          30           43.7 - 47.9  15.7 - 22.5, alternating

The two agree at low counts and part by a factor of two at high ones.
A GPU layer costs the page cache the CPU-side experts are read through:
30 layers wire 28.7 GiB, which with the ~15.5 GiB read through the cache
is 44.2 of 48 GiB - enough with nothing else resident, not enough with
the server and the runner beside it.  Wired GPU memory cannot be paged
out, so everything else gives way and the replies alternate between
~16 and ~22 tok/s as paging comes and goes.  The standalone figures are
reproducible (9 layers first and last in one run: 28.3 and 26.1), so
this is a benchmark leaving out part of the system it predicts, not
drift.

So the runner's tuner was right to keep 1 layer here, and its rule - a
busy SSD at the start count means walk towards fewer layers - reads this
Mac correctly.  LayerTuner is unchanged: a change to make it always
probe upwards first was written against the standalone curve's peak at
30 layers, which the server never sees, and reverted.

mac_split_bench.py says all this in its docstring now, and two real bugs
in it are fixed: it printed a "runner's count" computed differently from
the runner (26 against the runner's 10 for Qwen, ignoring the
START_GPU_SHARE path a model read from the SSD takes), and it left
--threads to llama.cpp instead of passing the runner's count, which on
an M5 Pro is worth about as much as the layer split.

Also measured: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ2_XS is not held back by the
28.8 GB per-layer embedding table the old handover suspected.  At 1 GPU
layer, where both methods agree, it reads 5.6 MB per token and writes
6.5 tok/s while Kolibri-1 reads a comparable 3.2 MB and writes 32.0 -
five times as fast with more active parameters per token (3.46B against
~2.4B).  What is left between them is the quantization: Q4_K_M scales
blocks, IQ2_XS looks codebook entries up.  A k-quant of the same model
(Q2_0) side by side would settle it and was not measured.

streams created cudaStreamNonBlocking, which do not wait for the legacy stream. A kernel enqueued right after could

the release that would carry the engine change), so until then setup behaves
as before and the golden configs are unchanged. Two tests run the new paths
with MIN_ENGINE patched; tools/test_setup_*.py pass (260 tests).

Resident RAM mode with a layer split

--resident-experts (the low-RAM mode's resident variant) ran as plain
--mmap-experts as soon as a layer split was set. It now keeps its RAM copy on
a split:

- the experts every stage's cache holds are left out of the RAM copy, not only
  CUDA0's;
- when the rest does not fit whole (#467), the copy keeps the hottest by the
  whole expert profile. Each stage only keeps its own layers' share of the
  profile, and ranked by CUDA0's share alone the copy held layers 0..K-1's
  experts and read every later layer's from the files (4.0 GiB in RAM instead
  of 21.2 on the PC below);
- an adaptive swap copies the evicted expert back into RAM from the cache of
  the card that owns its layer, on that card's stream. host_res holds slot
  numbers of whichever cache owns the layer: reading a later stage's slot out
  of CUDA0's cache put another expert's bytes in RAM, and after the first
  swaps the answers turned to garbage. (Latent until now: the guard kept the
  mode off a split.)
- the decode profile prints every stage's GPU profile, not only CUDA0's.

Remote expert caches (--expert-cache-remote) are still refused with it.

expert plan: a helper GPU's experts are not part of the PCIe share

The verify window's GPU plan counted a layer's misses and moved the last pcie_num/256 of them to the primary over PCIe,
leaving out the primary's resident experts and the peer tier's but not those a helper GPU (RemoteExperts) holds.  The
plan runs before RemoteExperts::begin(), which only claims rows the plan left at kind -1, so a PCIe share above 0 read
part of the helper's experts over the primary's link while the helper idled for them.

RemoteExperts::holds(layer, expert) (the helper cache's slot_of), and the plan treats such an expert as it treats the
peer tier's: not a miss, never in the PCIe share; its rows stay at kind -1 for begin().  No default changes.

README: the concurrency, the new flags, and what this fork changes

The README still described Strata as answering one request at a time with
--serve-slots as a footnote, which stopped being true. Adds a "Several chats at
once" section (slots, parking, the token budget, the fairness limit, the parking
RAM budget) and a "What's different here" section naming the fork's changes
against upstream.

The headline behaviour change is hold-don't-reject: a request blocked by
something that comes back - every slot busy, no free RAM for another
conversation, the mounted conversation mid-read, another slot holding the prompt
loan, an image request running alone - waits its turn and then runs, instead of
coming back with an error. Only a request that can NEVER run is refused on the
spot. Every wait is counted and visible: waiting=N on /status, /slots and
/metrics, and "slot 2 ran after waiting 1420 ms" in the log.

Flag defaults and the setup.py surface were checked against the source rather
than assumed: setup.py takes --serve-slots, --conversation-cache-mib and
--starve-ms, the rest go in the config's "args"; slots are validated against
slot::kMaxActive = 8 (generate.cpp:1422); the log line is quoted from
serve_driver.hpp:1142.

Also lands the S4.5 measurement, which corrects this repo's own earlier estimate
of what batching is worth:

  window_ms = 12.4 + (-0.016)*GPU-resident-row + 0.0601*CPU-pool-entry

A VRAM-resident expert row is free at this resolution; the whole 8-11 ms/row
slope is the 5-15% of routed experts that miss the expert cache and are computed
on the CPU pool. So the lever that flattens it is VRAM for the cache, not a
kernel rewrite: B=8 is +24% at today's 86.4% hit rate but +49% at a full cache.
docs/STAGE4-BATCH-DECODE.md 3.5/4.2 stay as the superseded estimate, with a
pointer to the new section 9.

The ceilings inventory was wrong too: 1.2 listed six hard 8-row limits, there
are thirteen, three of them silent, and GMAX at 24 stops the build outright
(ptxas: 0x10e00 > 0xc000). Priced in section 9.

All three reduced a row in TWO submits over a per-(row, lane) malloc_device

prefill: the dense GGUF projections through MMQ on HIP (opt-in STRATA_DENSE_MMQ=1), the K-quant instances on the HIP build

The prompt path's dense projections (attention qkv/gate, the PLE key, the shared
experts, the router, the head) run dequantize-to-FP16 + cuBLAS: on the RDNA2
cards that is 68% of the prefill GPU time at ~25% of the card's fp32-accumulate
rate, while the same shapes through llama.cpp's int8 MMQ run ~7x faster
(measured with bench_dense_gemm).  This wires Gemm::native's beta = 0 products
through the MMQ path the MoE experts already take: quantize the FP16 activations
to q8_1 (they are converted to FP32 in the dequant scratch, which the old path
only fills afterwards) and run one mul_mat_q product per 1024-row chunk.  It is
opt-in (STRATA_DENSE_MMQ=1; unset, nothing changes) and falls back silently to
the old path on any shape MMQ does not take.

- STRATA_MMQ_KQUANTS also compiles the Q4_K / Q5_K / Q5_1 / Q6_K instances on
  the HIP branch (the mixed-quant packs' dense tensors are K-quants: this
  model's attention/PLE matrices are IQ4_XS/IQ3_S/Q4_K/Q5_K/Q6_K), adds Q6_K to

V100 quant path: F32 routers and native Q8_0 hyper-connection projections

Two pack/runtime changes for the Volta (sm_70) target, where there is no
hardware BF16 path and every BF16 copy is re-rounded data the kernel widens
again on load.

F32 routers (iq_pack --compat-bf16): the 48 ffn_gate_inp.weight routers are
packed as F32 and dispatched through F32 MMVF GEMV (decode, verify, router
lookahead) and a cuBLAS FP32 GEMM (prefill).  The packed values are exactly
BF16-representable, so the F32 path reproduces the old BF16 router logits
bit-for-bit while dropping the repack.

Native GR (iq_pack --native-gr): the eight hyper-connection mixer projections
(hc_{attn,ffn}_{down,up,inject}, output_hc_{down,up}) take shape-only index
rows and are served straight from the GGUF Q8_0 bytes through the engine MMVQ
(gr_read GrNativeWeights on the FP32-activation kernels; prefill via
native_proj).  Q8_0 is 1.0625 B/elem against the BF16 copy's 2: the pack
arena drops 1.50 GiB -> 0.31 GiB.  Old packs keep working - a BF16 GR row
leaves the native skip set (the #326 ple_key rule, generalized) and the arena
serves it.

tok/s against 19.8-20.7 before, no regression; gr_parity clean, ctest unchanged

CPU expert kernels: gathered i-quant decodes, AVX-VNNI, IQ3_S for one token

In decode the CPU computes the experts no GPU cache holds. With Swift 1.5
IQ3_XXS on a 4060 Ti + 5080 that was the 5080 stage's largest wait, about 5 ms
of a 21 ms window. Three changes to the AVX-2 kernels, measured on a 14900KF:

- IQ3_S, IQ3_XXS and IQ2_S read their grid entries with one gather, from
  indices built in a register, on Intel P-cores only (CPUID 1Ah: the E-cores
  gather slower than they insert and keep the scalar decode). The same words
  reach the same lanes, so the products are bit for bit the same. Gate/up rows
  of one expert at three tokens on a P-core: IQ3_S 0.40 -> 0.27 ms, IQ2_S
  0.31 -> 0.27, IQ3_XXS 0.26 -> 0.24. IQ2_XXS was slower gathered and keeps
  its decode. STRATA_IQ_GATHER=0/1 forces it.
- AVX-VNNI (Alder Lake and later): vpdpwssd for the madd and add of every
  i-quant kernel, vpdpbusd for the maddubs and madd(ones) of the Q2_0 and
  IQ4_NL down rows. Integer sums, so again the same bits. Another 4-10% on a
  P-core, 15-25% on an E-core's Q2_0 down rows. STRATA_NO_AVXVNNI=1 turns it
  off.
- IQ3_S on an Intel CPU without AVX-512 takes the multi-token kernel for a
  single token too: 0.34 -> 0.19 ms per expert on a P-core, 0.71 -> 0.68 on an
  E-core, and most CPU experts in decode serve one token of the window. This
  one changes how those rows round (the #152 rule), the same way on every core.

Same engine, all three against none (IQ3_XXS at 160K, two alternating pairs):
the 5080 stage's CPU expert time 5.3 -> 4.8 ms per window, the window 21.2 ->
20.6 ms, code 135 -> 139 tok/s, prose 96 -> 98. With IQ2_XS the difference
stays within the noise.

--expert-profile-save: count the routing with the asynchronous tier

The learned profile ranks the experts by the routing the adaptive tier counted,
but only the blocking tier added its counts up. With --adapt-async 1 (the
default here) the saved profile held the residency and the loaded order only.
The asynchronous tier now adds the counts at the start of each round, before it
decays them, as the blocking one does.

Layer split: each card keeps only its own layers' weights

A split loaded the dense weights of all 48 layers on every card, though each card
runs only its own layers. Now every card loads them as before, the split is
decided, and each card reloads only its own layers' weights before the sessions
and the expert caches are made. The VRAM this frees goes to the expert caches.
The automatic split counts it when it places the boundary, so this also works
with --layer-split auto (upstream's #559 and #639 do it for explicit split
points). --no-trim-stage-weights keeps the old behaviour.

The PLE's six layer-1 weights are the only pointers into the old copy taken
before the split is known; they are wired again after the reload. The router
copy for the file tier's lookahead reads each layer's router from the card that
runs it.

On a 4060 Ti + 5080 at K=20 this frees 1.9 and 1.3 GiB. Same engine, without and
with trimming (code / prose at context 0, code / prose at 32K, 32K prompt):

  IQ2_XS:  162 / 109, 149 / 100, 1,899  ->  172 / 111, 157 / 104, 2,201 tok/s
  IQ3_XXS: 141 /  95,  98 /  71, 1,006  ->  144 /  97, 131 /  92, 1,978 tok/s

With IQ3_XXS at 160K the experts no card held did not all fit in RAM before, and
about 2,400 were read from the SSD per benchmark run; now none are. Teacher-forced
over 5,335 tokens, IQ3_XXS with and without trimming picks the same top token at
93.5% of the positions (perplexity 6.95 and 7.03).

PLE: the n-gram table in FP8 E4M3, as Qwen ships it

The engine read the 51.2e9-value n-gram table only as IQ4_NL (ISTA-DASLab's shard 2, 90 B/row), which is 8.1% off the
checkpoint's own values per row (correlation 0.996-0.997 on rows from all 128 shards: same table, same order). The
checkpoint stores it as 128 shards of [2500012, 160] F8_E4M3 plus one weight_scale.

- tools/ple_fp8_pack.py copies those bytes, unchanged, into a one-tensor GGUF: per_layer_token_embd.weight
  [160, 320001536] as I8, with strata.ple.format = f8_e4m3 and strata.ple.scale. 51.2 GB, streamed.
- PleTable opens either format; the row size (90 / 160) and the decode (IQ4_NL codebook / an E4M3 table times the
  scale) follow the file. PleReader takes the row size at open; its cache sizes itself by it. GGUF reader: type I8.
- A PLE-only table (architecture strata-ple) is not added to the dense-projection sources.
- The start line names the table's format.
- ple_fp8_parity: rows through Direct, Mmap and gather_batch match torch's decode of the checkpoint bit for bit.

First-token KL of the IQ4_NL table against the FP8 one: 0.0009 (1K), 0.0013 (2K), 0.0002 (4K), 0.022 (32K); mean 0.0061, top-1 4/4.

SSD keep-alive picks its page inside the table at the table's own row size; 0.1.31's shard list for the dense

diag(prefill): 选择重叠探针支持任意 tile 大小（STRATA_SEL_TILE）

原探针把 tile 固定为 16 个 query，故只能回答"16 query 共享 KV 能省多少"。
本改动把 tile 大小参数化（`STRATA_SEL_TILE`，默认 16，仅影响 `STRATA_SEL_OVERLAP=1`
时的调试输出，不设该 env 时行为逐字不变），于是可以量出**设计点**的读流量比。

实测（4K prompt，引擎真实选择；`并集/总和` 即共享 staging 后的读流量比）：

| 共享 KV 的 query 数 | 1（现状） | 2 | **4** | 8 | 16 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 读流量比 | 100.0% | 55.2% | **31.7%** | 18.2% | 9.2% |

即：**4 个 query 共享一次 KV staging 可把读流量降到 31.7%（3.15×）**，而 16 个可降到
9.2%（10.9×）。这为"prompt attention 多 query 共享 KV tile"的重写给出定量设计点：
现 kernel 每 block = 1 query × 12 head（smem `qh/ql[16][QS]` ≈ 16 KB，每 SM 2 block）；
改成 **4 query × 3 head**（head 槽位仍 12 个 ⇒ **smem 不变、占用率不变**）即可拿到 3.15×
的读流量下降 —— 该 kernel 目前正是被这些重复读限在 154 GB/s（见 bench/micro/qsa_prompt_attn_bench.cu）。

bench(sm75): 新增 prompt attention 微基准，并定位其真实瓶颈（KV 重复读）

新增 `bench/micro/qsa_prompt_attn_bench.cu`（复用 `qsa_prompt_attn_parity` 的输入搭建，
只加计时；`-DSTRATA_BUILD_TESTS=ON` 时构建，参数 `ctx nq reps`）。

实测（2×2080 Ti，24 heads / hd 256，单次 `qsa_prompt_attn_batch`）：
| ctx | cap | ms | 有效带宽 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1024 | 1024 | 2.65 | **406 GB/s** |
| 2048 | 2048 | 7.04 | 305 GB/s |
| 4096 | 2051 | 13.95 | **154 GB/s** |
| 8192 | 2051 | 14.04 | 153 GB/s |

时间随 `nq × cap` **严格线性**（nq 512/1024/2048 → 3.6/7.0/14.0 ms），但有效带宽随 cap
增大而塌陷：**瓶颈是每个 query 各自 gather 自己选中的 cell 造成的 KV 重复读** ——
ctx=1024 时 KV 池 6.3 MB 可进 L2（406 GB/s），ctx≥4096 时池 25 MB 超出 L2，2048 个 query
把同一批 cell 反复从 DRAM 读（2.15 GB/次），故只有 154 GB/s、0.31 TFLOP/s（fp16 峰值的 0.7%）。

结论：该 kernel **既非算力受限也非带宽上限**，而是被 gather 的重复读限住；对 cap 接近 ctx
（4K 档选择近乎稠密）的情形，改走"KV tile 常驻 smem、块内 query 共享"的稠密路径预计可把
DRAM 流量降约 3×（→ 时间约 5 ms/层）。属结构性改造，未在本轮落地，记入报告 §6.7。

perf(sm75): 稠密权重反量化改向量写（prompt +5%，数值逐位不变）

背景：`Gemm::native` 每次乘法前把原生量化块反量化到 scratch，prompt 路径的稠密投影
（Q5_K/Q6_K/IQ4_XS，形状 6144x2560 / 10240x2560 / 2560x640 等）都走它。原 kernel
每个线程算一个 32 元素组、用 put() **逐元素 2 字节写**：同一条 store 指令跨 lane 相距
64 字节 → 每条指令 32 个 2 字节事务。实测该 kernel 只跑到行带宽的约 18%。

改法（**数值逐位不变**：同样的算术、同样的顺序，只是把结果先写进寄存器缓冲再整体搬运）：
- `dequant_kernel` 增加模板参数 VEC：sm_75 用 `__align__(16) T buf[32]` + 4 次 uint4
  写（float 形式 8 次），其余架构保持原 kernel；
- 内层循环补 `#pragma unroll`，让缓冲留在寄存器而不是本地内存；
- 选择由 `tc_sm75_enabled(major, minor)` 决定 —— **只对 cc 7.5 生效**。

- prefill 28K 2,188-2,189 → **2,311 / 2,284**（+5.5%）

perf(sm75): 层切分下启用草稿层的批处理 prefill（每 chunk 省 ~90 ms，4K +3.4%）

根因：generate.cpp 里草稿层的 prompt 批处理被写成
  const bool batched = !multi_gpu && sp.draft_kv(...);
于是**任何层切分**都退回 drafter 自己的逐窗口 prefill。实测每 2,048-token chunk 花
98 ms 宿主串行时间，而同批 token 的 GPU 计算只需约 2 ms —— 即 12% 的 chunk 墙钟。

改法：draft_kv 用的是 mtp.kv_state_rw()（其 KV 属于**最后一张卡**，mtp.bind 绑定的也是
最后一张卡的权重与 head）+ Prefill 自己的 region/gemm/mmq_ctx，所以正确接线是**最后一张
stage 的 Prefill**（原代码用 sp = stage0，设备都不对，这大概就是当初用 !multi_gpu 关掉
它的原因）。单卡路径不变；批处理不可用时仍回退 mtp.prefill。

perf(sm75): prompt attention 单级缓冲 + 寄存器级软件流水

kv 缓冲不提供任何重叠，却让 smem 从 28.4KB 涨到 44.3KB（Turing 每 SM 64KB，

ple: keep the SSD awake while rows are read (STRATA_SSD_KEEPALIVE)

Some SSDs (here a WD_BLACK SN7100 on Windows 11) drop into a power state
after ~250 ms without a command and stall the next reads 50-150 ms; the
NVMe idle timeouts of Windows' power plan do not change it. In decode that
hits the first read after a pause: at the start of a request, or after a
few rounds whose rows all came from the row cache. --ple-io ram, which
avoids the reads altogether, is not available on Windows.

The reader's worker now reads one page of the table (a different one each
time) when no read has gone out for 100 ms, until 60 s after the last
issue; then the SSD may sleep until the next request re-arms it. A
keep-alive read counts when it completes and stays out of the row-read
counters and latencies; the "ple io" line adds "SSD kept awake by N reads
(slowest X ms)". A keep-alive read that fails, or cannot be submitted,
turns the keep-alive off instead of failing the reader.
STRATA_SSD_KEEPALIVE=0 turns it off, =50 shortens the period;
STRATA_SSD_KEEPALIVE_WINDOW sets the window in seconds. Only with the I/O
worker (the default), not with --ple-sync-submit or --ple-io mmap/ram.

The reader's statistics are now copied and reset under the worker's lock
(snapshot()), since the worker may be counting a keep-alive read. The
selftest checks the period, the window, the re-arm by a ticket the row
cache serves, that rows and read counters are untouched, and that the
caller-thread mode has none.

A scan on that PC (reads after pauses of every length): 0 of 211 bursts
stalled after pauses under 200 ms, 35 of 73 after 200 ms and more, 0 of 68
of those with the keep-alive on.

hc: the multi-token hyper-connection read split finer, checked bit for bit on each card (STRATA_HC_V2)

The multi-token read (verify windows, the MTP drafter) keeps v1's
arithmetic exactly - every sum over the same elements in the same order -
and only splits the work differently:
- the norm (v2, v3): one block per token and stream instead of one per
  token. Each thread visits the elements of its stream in the order it did
  in v1, so every sum of squares and rs is v1's; R' * w_norm is recomputed
  and scaled once (the same two roundings as v1's store and in-place
  scale). On an RTX 4080 SUPER: 0.58 -> 0.23 ms per 4-token round.
- the down projection (v3): v1's rows per block and lane order, but the
  activations arrive by cp.async in half-stream tiles, two in flight, in a
  bank-conflict-free two-plane layout, and the next tile's weights load
  while the current one is used. A tile is 160 = 5 x 32 chunks, so a lane
  still accumulates its chunks lane + 32 q in ascending order. Before sm_80
  and on HIP the staging is a plain copy (the same bits).

Verifier::init runs fused_gr_check once per card: v1, v2, v3 and the
single-token read on random bf16 weights and inputs (1..8 tokens, with and
without the pending write), every output compared bit for bit; the newest
variant that agrees runs on that card and the log says which. A card that
has not been checked runs v1. STRATA_HC_V2=0 keeps v1, =2 stops at v2.
The down kernels carry as many tokens per launch as the card's shared
memory allows (v3: 10 KB per token), as v1 did.

serve: keep retained K/V through the cache capacity gate

park_current dropped the retained K/V whenever can_fit failed and fell
back to a full snapshot capture. The gate duplicates what make_room
decides immediately after, with harsher arithmetic: the slot term fires
when make_room enforces the same cap, and the byte term compares the
with-reuse estimate against headroom that ignores the parked image
replacing the retained buffers. make_room already implements the
stated policy - pressure drops the optional retained storage before
evicting any parked conversation (the priority the cache tests pin).
With a full cache the fallback buys nothing: the fresh estimate forces
the same or more eviction, plus a whole-snapshot recapture instead of
the growth - hundreds of ms per park at ~100K tokens where one long
conversation round-trips while short-lived conversations keep the
cache full.

The with-reuse estimate stays uncapped: it counts the retained buffers'
capacity and directories, and put() charges that same true size, so a
capped figure would under-evict and overfill the budget.

(~48 registers; the default verify window, --spec 4 with the split off, fits
in one pass).

kernels: faster grouped and per-hit Q2_0 expert kernels, bitwise identical

The grouped kernels (verify window, MTP layer) staged each entry's activations
as xs_q[k][c * 8 + j], an 8-way bank conflict on every read, and recomputed the
chunk sum hx with eight dp4a for every row. The per-hit kernels (token graph)
read each chunk with 44 byte loads.

New kernels, on by default:
- activations regrouped once per chunk so the codes expand with shift+mask
  and hx is summed once per chunk;
- grouped: word-major shared layout xs_w[j][k * NC + c] plus (dx, hx) pairs,
  conflict-free on the staging writes and the reads, two rows per warp;
- per hit: nine aligned word loads per activation chunk, uint2 code loads,
  16-bit scale loads, one warp per (gate, up) pair or pair of down rows.

every output matches the previous kernels bit for bit. STRATA_OLD_GROUPED=1
(or moe_grouped_select_old(1)) selects the previous kernels, and so does any

Multi-GPU: the session carve and the per-stage prompt loans

Two things a layer split was paying for and not using.

* THE SESSION CARVE.  A stage carved state for ALL 48 layers whatever slice it ran - every QSA KV pool at
  max_cells, every GDN recurrence - the whole-model-sized-buffer disease the chunked-QSA-prefill PR cured
  upstream.  `session_bytes`/`session_init` take [layer_lo, layer_hi), and a session now owns only that range:
  `qsa_states`/`gdn_state` keep GLOBAL ordinal indexing and simply hold fewer rows (`qsa_ord0`/`qsa_alloc`,
  `gdn_ord0`/`gdn_alloc`), per-layer consumers subtract `gdn_ord0`, and the model-level uses - the shared RoPE
  table, the prefill staging identity, the MTP rope borrow - read `qsa_states[qsa_primary()]`.  A range with no
  QSA layer still carves ONE primary state so those uses stay valid, and the default full range is
  byte-identical to the old carve.  On the 2x3060 + 2x5060 rig, CUDA1's [30, 48) session costs 0.93 GiB:
  7.83 GiB free before the carve, 6.90 GiB after (`session [30, 48) and the head`).

* PER-STAGE PROMPT LOANS.  `no_prefill_borrow = true` for split stages said "each stage's prompt path has its
  own buffers" - true, but that is a reason to give each stage its own LOAN, not to make every stage withhold a
  chunk-sized reserve from its cache for the whole session, and forced on it also collapsed `--prefill auto` to
  2048.  Each prompt path now borrows the tail of ITS OWN stage's cache (`PfPart`), so outside the prompt the
  whole cache is expert cache: `--prefill auto` is the largest chunk every participant can lend (8192 tokens
  here), a participant refills its loan into its own slots and marks only its own layers (a slot refilled into
  another cache, or another stage's rows marked resident, is silent and produces plausible tokens), and the
  chunk is the largest one EVERY participant can lend rather than one card's answer imposed on the others.
  A participant that cannot lend the buffers falls back to the prompt path's own, as a lone one always could;
  with a single participant the plan reduces to `plan_lend` exactly, so the single-GPU loan is unchanged from
  main - the percentage cap stays an AUTO-chunk rule (an explicit `--prefill` is the operator's number and a
  loan of it only has to leave the 128-slot floor).  The flat 1 GiB withheld from every stage after the first
  becomes what is actually held back after the weights, session and drafter exist: 96 MiB of verify windows,
  plus 1000 MiB of drafter and head on the ONE stage that carries them.  CUDA0 lends 2162 slots (3.98 GiB),
  CUDA1 1993 of its 2653 (3.97 GiB).

* REPORTING.  `expert_slots`/`expert_cache_mib` sum every tier: a 4-GPU 256K run reported CUDA0's cache alone
  (3327 experts) while the four cards held 13310, so the Monitor tab was wrong by 4x for every multi-GPU
  config.  `expert_slots_primary`/`expert_cache_primary_mib` keep the old figure.  The helper ranks'
  ms_begin/ms_wait are cumulative since boot and were printed next to per-request deltas; they take deltas now.
  KV-streaming stats iterate the session's OWNED ordinals.

* REFUSALS.  `--gpu-only-full` and `--gpu-stages` replay every layer through CUDA0's session, which a split
  carves to CUDA0's range, so they are refused with a layer split rather than answering about another stage's
  state; the token-graph hit path is disabled under a split (such a graph cannot span stages); and the sessions
  are allocated AFTER the split search, because the search prices each placement by what that range's session
  will cost on that device (`session_bytes` is pure arithmetic).

Pascal (sm_60): bring the engine up on compute capability 6.0

Two gates stand between this engine and a 6.0 card, plus one attribute the card does
not honour.  None of them needs the kernels rewritten:

* `CMakeLists.txt` refuses to configure below sm_75;
* `__dp4a` (6.1+) appears 29 times in the i-quant kernels (`native_mmvq.cu`,
  `s2_expert_grouped.cu`, `iq_kernels.cu`) and `__nanosleep` (7.0+) in the three
  doorbell waits (`elementwise.cu`, `verify_kernels.cu`);
* the Turing port sizes `fused_gr_read_multi`'s slice from
  `cudaDevAttrMaxSharedMemoryPerBlockOptin`, which on an sm_60 answers 65536 - a card
  whose launch validator enforces the 49152 B per-block limit instead.  The capacity
  comes out 6 tokens and every 6- or 8-token window fails the launch with
  "invalid argument".

## The changes

* **`include/strata/kernels/dp4a.hpp` (new)** - `STRATA_DP4A` and `strata_spin_pause()`.
  The dp4a fallback is llama.cpp's own (`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/common.cuh`): both operands
  read as SIGNED bytes, accumulated into int32 - which is what `__dp4a` does for exactly
  these call sites, the kernels here being transcribed from `vecdotq.cuh`/`mmvq.cu`.  The
  fallback is bit-exact, not approximate; the nanosleep sites only pace single-thread
  doorbell waits, so on sm_6x the loop spins.  Both are `__CUDA_ARCH__` selections, so a
  HIP build takes neither: its `__dp4a` and `__nanosleep` are `hip_compat`'s own.
* **`CMakeLists.txt`** - `-DSTRATA_EXPERIMENTAL_SM60=ON` relaxes the architecture gate,
  and the refusal message names it.  The UTF-8 BOM stays.
* **`fused_gr.cu`** - below sm_70 the slice capacity comes from
  `cudaDevAttrMaxSharedMemoryPerBlock` (49152 B -> 4 tokens) instead of the opt-in.  The
  Turing port's slicing, its no-opt-in fallback and the HIP expression are unchanged.

On sm_70 and newer this is a no-op: the opt-in is honoured there, so the capacity is the
value it already was, and `STRATA_DP4A` and `strata_spin_pause()` compile to `__dp4a` and
`__nanosleep` exactly as before.  Building for a 6.0 card needs a CUDA release that still
targets Pascal (CUDA 13 removed it; 12.x has compute_60), and `CMAKE_CUDA_STANDARD` has
to stay 17 for it: nvcc 12.9 refuses `-std=c++20` when the host compiler is VS2019's `cl`
and silently falls back to C++14, which rejects the nested
`namespace strata::kernels {` declarations.

fix: harden multi-session lane scheduling after affinity overwrite regression

The first session-affinity hotfix stored only one affinity key per lane. A short unrelated request could therefore reuse a lane after a long turn completed, overwrite that key, and make the long conversation's next turn route to another GPU and pay a full prompt re-prefill.

Replace per-lane single-owner affinity with a bounded session-to-lane LRU map. Keep busy lifetime request/stream-scoped and affinity lifetime session-scoped. Existing sessions wait for their remembered eligible lane instead of spilling. New sessions never enter a busy lane; among idle eligible lanes they prefer an empty live slot, then the smallest live request state, then the least recently used live state, with rotating order as the final fairness tie-breaker. The policy is hardware-agnostic and contains no GPU-index/model/PCIe-width hardcoding.

Add regression coverage for all-busy queueing, long-session affinity surviving intervening short sessions, live-state-aware placement, bounded affinity state, and vision rebinding. serve: the conversation cache keeps its shared prefix; the rest rotates LRU

The retained checkpoints are always a prefix chain - the request loop drops
any checkpoint that is not a prefix of the current prompt, because its
positional cells are gone (the KV cache is one arena, one branch of history
at a time).  A radix cache's tree collapsed onto the one branch the session
can hold, and the chain's root is the node a radix cache keeps while its
leaves rotate: in practice the end of the system prompt, which every new
chat of the same client mounts through.

First-in-first-out kept that node only by accident of being first: after
prompt_cache newer checkpoints it was gone, and the next chat re-read the
whole prefix at prefill speed (~30 s per 30K tokens).  Now the root is
pinned while the budget allows root and leaf apart (cap >= 2; below that
the old behaviour stands), the rest rotates by least recent use, and a
mount re-dates the checkpoint it mounted through.

The policy is one pure function (conv_cache.hpp) with its scenarios in
conv_cache_test.cpp; checkpoint_save/restore and the state format are
untouched, so STRATA_CKPT_REREAD's token-for-token guarantee holds.
